judgments.forked_readings_summary: All four read the task identically: build a net-new (scaffold-api, explicitly NOT a migration) synchronous REST/JSON HTTP service for customer commerce orders, with CRUD-plus-lifecycle endpoints (create/read/list/update-status/cancel) over an Order resource (id, customer ref, line items, status enum, totals, timestamps), backed by a relational persistence layer with migrations. Core behaviors agree precisely: server-side validation rejecting bad payloads with 4xx before persisting, server-computed totals never trusted from client, server-assigned id, 404 on unknown id, a status state machine where illegal transitions return 409, pagination on list, and durable persistence. Surfaces agree (controller/routing, service/domain, data-access/repo, DTO/wire-format, validation, tests). Assumptions converge tightly (relational DB, single-service, repo's dotnet-service generation spec as default stack, payment/inventory/async-events out of scope). Only minor variations: (a) AUTH — reading #2 treats an auth boundary as an in-scope (stubbed) surface and assumes AuthN/Z required on write endpoints, whereas #1/#3/#4 explicitly place auth out of scope (auth seam only); all agree it is not the core deliverable. (b) API DOCUMENTATION — #1 and #3 explicitly list OpenAPI/Swagger as in-scope; #2 mentions a documented wire contract + run instructions; #4 omits docs entirely. (c) Atomic/transactional writes are stressed by #1/#2 but merely not-contradicted by #3/#4. None of these alter the central deliverable; they are detail/emphasis differences, so the readings describe the same task.

All four read the SAME task: build a net-new RESTful HTTP/JSON service for managing customer (e-commerce) orders — CRUD-plus-lifecycle (create, read, list, update-status, cancel) over an Order resource with line items, backed by a relational DB via a repository layer, scaffolded from scratch (scaffold-api, explicitly NOT a migration). Scope boundary is unanimous: single service, single DB; payments, inventory, async/events, and multi-service orchestration are out. Surfaces are unanimous: HTTP controller/route layer, service/domain layer (server-side total computation + status state machine), data-access layer + schema/migrations, JSON DTO/wire-format + validation, and a test surface. Core behaviors are unanimous and even share specific non-obvious details: order totals computed server-side and never trusted from the client, status transitions enforced by a state machine (illegal → 409), 404 on unknown id, 4xx (not 500) on invalid payloads, server-assigned id, atomic order+line-items persistence, paginated list. The ONLY genuine divergence is auth as an assumption: reading 2 treats AuthN/Z as in-scope (required on mutating endpoints, stubbed boundary acceptable) and lists an 'Auth boundary' comparison surface, while readings 1, 3, and 4 explicitly place auth OUT of scope for the initial scaffold (leave an auth seam, do not implement identity). That is a minor 3-vs-1 split on one secondary surface that all four flag as an assumption, not a difference in the primary deliverable. A trivial cancel-mechanism variation (soft status=cancelled vs hard DELETE) also exists but every reading lists both as options. Net: same task, one minor auth-assumption variation.

All four read the task identically: build a net-new RESTful HTTP/JSON service for customer (e-commerce) orders, with CRUD-plus-lifecycle operations (create/read/list/update-status/cancel) over an Order resource with line items, backed by a relational persistence layer with migrations. All four explicitly assume net-new scaffold-api (NOT migration), follow the repo's configured generation spec (dotnet-service), and treat synchronous REST/JSON (not gRPC/GraphQL/event), single-service/single-DB, with payment/inventory/notifications out of scope.

Surfaces match across all four: HTTP controller/routing, service/domain layer, data-access/repository over a DB, wire-format/DTO/serialization, validation, and tests. Differences are only sub-surface granularity (e.g., #1 and #3 break out app bootstrap/config and OpenAPI docs as distinct surfaces; #4 lists error/status-mapping separately) — not scope differences.

Core behaviors are in lockstep: validate input and reject with 4xx before persisting; compute order total server-side (never trust the client); server-assigned id; 404 on unknown id; status state-machine enforcing legal transitions (illegal → 409); durable/atomic persistence; correct HTTP semantics (201 on create, etc.).

The single divergence is auth treatment, and it is minor: #1 and #4 put authN/Z explicitly OUT of scope (unless requested), #3 leaves an auth seam without implementing, and #2 says auth is required on mutating endpoints but stubbed/pluggable for the first iteration and lists it as a comparison surface. Because #2 only wants a stubbed/pluggable seam for the first cut, the practical first-iteration behavior (a seam, no real identity scheme) is nearly identical to #3's — so this is a minor variation, not a material fork.
